title: The Same Camera
passage:
Daichi used to believe that taking good photographs required an expensive camera. He enjoyed looking at travel photos online and often compared them with pictures from his phone. His own photos seemed ordinary, so he assumed the device was the problem. During a family trip, Daichi's aunt, who enjoyed photography, asked to use his phone for a few minutes. She took pictures of the same park that Daichi had photographed earlier. When they compared the images, Daichi was surprised. Her photos looked more interesting even though she had used exactly the same phone. His aunt explained that she usually thought about three things before pressing the button. First, she looked at the direction of the light. Second, she decided what the main subject was. Third, she checked the edges of the picture for objects that might distract the viewer. They practiced together. Instead of photographing an entire garden, Daichi chose one bench with yellow leaves around it. He moved a few steps to avoid a trash can in the background. Then he waited until a cloud changed the light. The result was much better than his first photo. After returning home, Daichi continued practicing with ordinary places. He photographed his bicycle, a cup on the kitchen table, and the path to school. Because the subjects were familiar, he could focus on composition rather than searching for something unusual. A few weeks later, he looked at his older photographs again. He noticed that many of them did not have a clear subject. He had often tried to include everything he could see. His newer pictures were simpler. He started printing one photo each week and writing a short note about the choice that had improved it. Sometimes the note was about light; sometimes it was about moving closer or waiting for a person to leave the background. Daichi still hoped to buy a better camera someday, but he no longer believed equipment alone would solve his problem. A tool could improve image quality, yet it could not decide where to stand, what to include, or when to wait. Those choices belonged to the person taking the picture. Learning to notice light, space, and unnecessary details had improved his photography more than buying a new device would have.

His aunt later asked Daichi to choose three photographs for a family album. Surprisingly, the sharpest picture was not his favorite. He selected images that clearly showed a moment or feeling. That experience taught him that technical quality matters, but a photograph also succeeds by directing attention and telling a simple visual story.
translation:
大地は以前、よい写真を撮るには高価なカメラが必要だと思っていました。旅行写真を見ては自分のスマートフォン写真と比べ、平凡に見える原因は機材だと考えていたのです。家族旅行のとき、写真好きの叔母が大地のスマートフォンで同じ公園を撮りました。すると、同じ機器なのに叔母の写真の方がずっと魅力的でした。叔母は、撮る前に三つ考えると言います。光の向き、主役となるもの、そして写真の端に邪魔な物が入っていないかです。二人は一緒に練習しました。庭全体を撮る代わりに黄色い葉に囲まれたベンチを主役にし、背景のごみ箱が入らないよう数歩動き、雲によって光が変わるのを待ちました。帰宅後も大地は、自転車、台所のカップ、通学路など身近な物を撮り続けました。見慣れた対象だからこそ、珍しい場所探しではなく構図に集中できました。数週間後、昔の写真を見ると、何でも画面に入れようとして主役が分からなくなっていたことに気づきます。そこで毎週一枚を印刷し、何を工夫したか短いメモを書くようにしました。光についての週もあれば、近づいたことや背景から人がいなくなるまで待ったことを書く週もありました。大地はいつか良いカメラを買いたいとは思っていますが、機材だけで問題が解決するとは考えなくなりました。画質は道具で向上しても、どこに立つか、何を入れるか、いつ待つかを決めるのは撮影する人です。光や空間、不要なものに気づく力こそが、機材購入以上に写真を上達させたのでした。

後日、叔母は家族アルバムに入れる写真を三枚選ぶよう大地に頼みました。意外にも、最も鮮明な写真が一番好きとは限りませんでした。大地は瞬間や気持ちがよく伝わる写真を選び、技術的な画質だけでなく、見る人の注意を導き、簡単な物語を伝えることも写真の大切な役割だと学びました。
